title: Ensemble Learning - Overview
abstract:
A single decision tree is prone to overfitting, so combine several models
instead. This document covers the wisdom of the crowd that underpins ensembles,
the requirement that base models be different, the majority-vote and
averaging rules for classification and regression, the two mathematical results
that explain why ensembles work at all — Condorcet's jury theorem and the
variance-of-an-average formula — and the four families the notes name: voting,
bagging, boosting and stacking.

blocks.t: Why It Works

blocks.cap:
The two mathematical results behind ensembles. Left: majority voting
 amplifies an advantage — but only if each model is better than chance. Right:
 averaging reduces variance — but only to the extent the models are
 decorrelated.

blocks.t: Result 1 — Condorcet's Jury Theorem

Suppose $M$ independent models each classify correctly with probability
$p$. The majority vote is correct with probability
P_{\text{ensemble}}=\sum_{k=\lfloor M/2\rfloor+1}^{M}\binom{M}{k}p^{k}(1-p)^{M-k}.

items:
If $p<0.5$, then $P_{\text{ensemble}}\to0$ — the ensemble is
 worse than any single model.

blocks.t: Result 2 — the variance of an average
For $B$ models each with variance $\sigma^2$ and pairwise correlation $\rho$:

The second term vanishes as $B\to\infty$; the first does not. So adding
more models helps only until the correlation floor is reached.

And the bias of the average is the average of the biases — averaging does
nothing for bias. That single fact explains the whole design of bagging
(Topic 60): it needs low-bias, high-variance base models, and it needs
them decorrelated.
Why the notes insist the models be "different kind"

Both results assume the models are not making the same mistakes. If four identical
trees vote, the majority is whatever that one tree said — $\rho=1$, and the
variance formula gives no reduction at all.

Diversity is therefore engineered deliberately, and the four families differ
precisely in how:

rows: Different algorithms — logistic regression, KNN, a tree
Different data — each model sees a bootstrap sample
Different data and different features per split
Different focus — each model targets the previous one's errors
A meta-model learns how to combine them

blocks.t: The Four Families

blocks.cap: The taxonomy from the notes, with the topics that cover each.

blocks.t: The bias–variance reading

Topic 40 named regularisation, bagging and boosting as the three routes to the
sweet spot. Two of the three are here, and they attack different terms:

items:
Bagging averages away variance, so it wants base models
 that are low-bias, high-variance — fully grown trees.

Boosting composes away bias, so it wants base models that
 are high-bias, low-variance — decision stumps.

blocks.t:
That is why the two use opposite base learners, and it is the single most useful
thing to remember about them.
Costs

head: Advantages
Disadvantages
rows: More accurate than a single model — ensembles win most competitions
Interpretability is lost: 500 trees cannot be read like one
More stable — less sensitive to the particular sample

blocks.t: An ensemble cannot rescue a bad base model

Condorcet requires $p>0.5$. If your base models are worse than random — or all
wrong in the same way, because a feature is missing or the labels are noisy —
the ensemble amplifies the error rather than cancelling it. Ensembling is a
variance-and-bias technique, not a substitute for the feature engineering of
Part II.
Code

import numpy as np
from math import comb
from sklearn.ensemble import (VotingClassifier, BaggingClassifier,
                              RandomForestClassifier, AdaBoostClassifier,
                              GradientBoostingClassifier, StackingClassifier)
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.naive_bayes import GaussianNB
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split, cross_val_score

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
n = 2000
X = rng.normal(0, 1, (n, 12))
y = (X[:, 0] + 0.8*X[:, 1] - 0.5*X[:, 2] + 0.4*X[:, 0]*X[:, 1]
     + rng.normal(0, 1.1, n) > 0).astype(int)
X_tr, X_te, y_tr, y_te = train_test_split(X, y, test_size=.3,
                                          stratify=y, random_state=0)

# =====================================================================
# 1. CONDORCET'S JURY THEOREM
# =====================================================================
def majority_accuracy(p, M):
    return sum(comb(M, k) * p**k * (1-p)**(M-k) for k in range(M//2 + 1, M + 1))

print(f"{'models':>7s} " + "".join(f"{f'p={p}':>9s}" for p in [0.45, 0.55, 0.60, 0.70]))
for M in [1, 3, 11, 51, 101]:
    print(f"{M:7d} " + "".join(f"{majority_accuracy(p, M):9.4f}"
                               for p in [0.45, 0.55, 0.60, 0.70]))
# p=0.60: 11 models -> 0.75, 101 models -> 0.98.
# p=0.45: MORE models make it WORSE. The base model must beat chance.

# =====================================================================
# 2. THE MAJORITY VOTE AND THE AVERAGE
# =====================================================================
preds = np.array(["hoga", "hoga", "hoga", "nahi hoga"])
vals, counts = np.unique(preds, return_counts=True)
print(f"\nclassification: {dict(zip(vals, counts))} -> "
      f"'{vals[counts.argmax()]}'  [majority count]")

ages = np.array([21, 23, 31, 40])
print(f"regression: {ages.tolist()} -> {ages.mean():.2f}  [average]")

# =====================================================================
# 3. DIVERSITY IS EVERYTHING -- the variance formula
# =====================================================================
def var_of_average(rho, B):
    return rho + (1 - rho) / B                  # as a fraction of a single model

print(f"\n{'rho':>6s} " + "".join(f"{f'B={B}':>9s}" for B in [5, 25, 100, 1000]))
for rho in [0.0, 0.3, 0.6, 0.9, 1.0]:
    print(f"{rho:6.1f} " + "".join(f"{var_of_average(rho, B):9.4f}"
                                   for B in [5, 25, 100, 1000]))
# rho=1.0 (identical models): variance NEVER falls, whatever B.
# rho=0.0 (independent):      variance falls as 1/B.

# IDENTICAL MODELS GAIN NOTHING -- demonstrated:
same = VotingClassifier([(f"t{i}", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0))
                         for i in range(5)], voting="hard")
diff = VotingClassifier([(f"t{i}", DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=i,
                                                          max_features=4))
                         for i in range(5)], voting="hard")
print(f"\n5 IDENTICAL trees : {cross_val_score(same, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
print(f"5 DIFFERENT trees : {cross_val_score(diff, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
print(f"1 tree alone      : "
      f"{cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 4. ALL FOUR FAMILIES
# =====================================================================
base_models = [
    ("lr",  make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000))),
    ("knn", make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(15))),
    ("dt",  DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=6, random_state=0)),
    ("nb",  GaussianNB()),
]

ensembles = {
    "single tree":  DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0),
    "VOTING":       VotingClassifier(base_models, voting="soft"),
    "BAGGING":      BaggingClassifier(DecisionTreeClassifier(),
                                      n_estimators=100, random_state=0),
    "random forest": RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
    "BOOSTING (ada)": AdaBoostClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0),
    "BOOSTING (gb)":  GradientBoostingClassifier(random_state=0),
    "STACKING":     StackingClassifier(base_models,
                                       final_estimator=LogisticRegression(),
                                       cv=5),
}
print(f"\n{'model':18s} {'cv accuracy':>13s}")
for name, m in ensembles.items():
    s = cross_val_score(m, X_tr, y_tr, cv=5, n_jobs=-1)
    print(f"{name:18s} {s.mean():8.4f} +/- {s.std():.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 5. EACH BASE MODEL MUST BE DIFFERENT -- measure the disagreement
# =====================================================================
fitted = [(name, m.fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)) for name, m in base_models]
print(f"\npairwise DISAGREEMENT between base models:")
print(f"{'':6s}" + "".join(f"{n:>7s}" for n, _ in fitted))
for n1, p1 in fitted:
    print(f"{n1:6s}" + "".join(f"{(p1 != p2).mean():7.3f}" for _, p2 in fitted))
# Off-diagonal entries near 0 mean the models are redundant -- adding both
# to a vote buys nothing. Larger values are what you want.

print(f"\n{'':22s} {'accuracy':>9s}")
for n_, p_ in fitted:
    print(f"{n_:22s} {(p_ == y_te).mean():9.4f}")
votes = np.array([p for _, p in fitted])
maj = (votes.mean(axis=0) >= 0.5).astype(int)
print(f"{'majority of the four':22s} {(maj == y_te).mean():9.4f}")

# =====================================================================
# 6. BAGGING ATTACKS VARIANCE, BOOSTING ATTACKS BIAS
# =====================================================================
print(f"\n{'base learner':26s} {'alone':>8s} {'bagged':>9s} {'boosted':>9s}")
for tag, depth in [("deep tree  (low bias)", None), ("stump      (high bias)", 1)]:
    alone = cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth, random_state=0),
                            X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    bag = cross_val_score(BaggingClassifier(
              DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth), n_estimators=100,
              random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    boo = cross_val_score(AdaBoostClassifier(
              DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=depth or 3), n_estimators=100,
              random_state=0), X_tr, y_tr, cv=5).mean()
    print(f"{tag:26s} {alone:8.4f} {bag:9.4f} {boo:9.4f}")
# Bagging helps the DEEP tree most (it had the variance).
# Boosting helps the STUMP most (it had the bias).

# =====================================================================
# 7. THE COST
# =====================================================================
import time, pickle
print(f"\n{'model':18s} {'fit time':>10s} {'artefact':>12s} {'readable?':>11s}")
for name, m in [("single tree", DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=4, random_state=0)),
                ("forest (200)", RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200,
                                                        random_state=0))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter(); m.fit(X_tr, y_tr); el = time.perf_counter() - t0
    size = len(pickle.dumps(m)) / 1024
    readable = "yes" if name == "single tree" else "no"
    print(f"{name:18s} {el:9.3f}s {size:10.1f} KB {readable:>11s}")

# =====================================================================
# 8. AN ENSEMBLE CANNOT RESCUE A BAD BASE MODEL
# =====================================================================
y_noise = rng.integers(0, 2, len(y_tr))          # labels with NO signal
print(f"\non pure-noise labels:")
print(f"  single tree : {cross_val_score(DecisionTreeClassifier(), X_tr, y_noise, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
print(f"  forest (500): {cross_val_score(RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=500, random_state=0), X_tr, y_noise, cv=5).mean():.4f}")
# Both ~0.50. Ensembling reduces variance and bias -- it cannot create signal
# that the features do not contain (the Bayes-error argument, Topic 05).
Worked Examples
How much a majority vote can gain
Suppose each of $n$ classifiers is correct with probability $p=0.7$, and their errors are independent. A majority vote is correct when more than half of them are correct.
Three classifiers. Majority correct if $\ge 2$ are correct:
Five classifiers. Majority correct if $\ge 3$ are correct:
P \approx 0.837
Reading it. Individually each model is right 70% of the time. Combining three gives 78.4%, and five gives 83.7%. The gain comes from errors cancelling out.

The catch. The calculation assumes independent errors. Real models trained on the same data make correlated mistakes, so the gain is much smaller. This is why ensembles deliberately diversify their members: bootstrap samples (bagging), feature subsets (random forests), or different algorithms (voting, stacking).
Summary
Everything on one page

items:
A single decision tree is prone to overfitting, thus an ensemble
 is more accurate. Ensemble learning means combining multiple ML
 models.

Wisdom of the Crowd — the crowd knows better — is the
 backbone of ensembles.

Each base model should be different. Identical models give
 $\rho=1$ and no benefit whatsoever.

Classification: majority count. Regression: average of all the
 models.

Condorcet's jury theorem: with independent models each better
 than chance, majority accuracy $\to1$ as the count grows — and $\to0$ if
 they are worse than chance.

Variance of an average:
 $\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$. Only the second term vanishes,
 so diversity sets the floor. Bias is unchanged by averaging.

Four families: Voting Ensemble, Bagging (with
 Random Forest), Boosting (AdaBoost, 
 Gradient Boosting, XGBoost), and Stacking.

Bagging attacks variance and wants deep trees; boosting attacks
 bias and wants stumps.

We use ensemble learning mostly every time in practice. The cost
 is interpretability, compute and artefact size.

blocks.t: Questions you will actually be asked
Q. Why does combining models help?

Two reasons. Majority voting amplifies a per-model advantage — Condorcet's
theorem — provided each model beats chance. And averaging reduces variance by
$\rho\sigma^2+\frac{1-\rho}{B}\sigma^2$, so independent errors cancel while the
shared signal survives.
Q. Why must the base models be different?

Because the variance of their average is floored at $\rho\sigma^2$. With identical
models $\rho=1$ and there is no reduction at all — the ensemble is just the one
model, computed $B$ times. Every ensemble method is really a technique for
engineering diversity.
Q. Can an ensemble be worse than a single model?

Yes. If the base models are worse than random, Condorcet works in reverse and
majority voting drives accuracy towards zero. Ensembling also cannot create
information the features do not contain — on pure-noise labels, 500 trees score
exactly what one does.
Q. Bagging or boosting?

They fix different problems. Bagging reduces variance, so use it when a single
model overfits — and give it deep, high-variance base learners. Boosting reduces
bias, so use it when a single model underfits — and give it shallow,
high-bias learners like stumps.
Q. What do you give up by using an ensemble?

Interpretability above all: you can read one tree and not five hundred. Also
$B\times$ the training and inference cost, a much larger artefact, and more
hyperparameters. Where a regulator must be given reasons, a single model or a
linear one often wins despite lower accuracy.
Q. Why do random forests sample features as well as rows?

To lower $\rho$. Bootstrapping the rows alone leaves the trees quite correlated,
because a strong feature is chosen at the root of nearly every tree. Sampling
features at each split forces different trees to use different predictors, which
pushes the variance floor down (Topic 61).
